messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] interval mapping in an intercross
parts:
R/qtl doesn't currently include facilities to do interval mapping for segregation distortion.

I would look carefully at the genotype frequencies in both the long- and short-lived individuals at the markers where you see deviation from the expected frequencies in the long-lived individuals. Is there real evidence for these markers being associated with longevity, or are the regions showing segregation distortion in all individuals?

karl


On Dec 7, 2012, at 6:46 PM, dario <drval...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> I am mapping longevity in a F2-intercross. The distribution of phenotypes in the F2 is bimodal, with two peaks, one corresponding the peak of survival of the short-lived P0, and the other corresponding to the peak in survival of the long-lived. I selectively genotyped my F2, prioritizing the long-lived F2 over the short-lived, since I believe most of the statistical power should come from the long-lived individuals (there are several reasons why a fish can die young).
> When I ran scanone over the whole genotyped cross, I did not find any significant QTL. I ran a likelihood ratio test in the longest-lived individuals, testing the probability that the observed allelic frequencies at each marker were significantly different from 0.5. In this way I found 24 significant markers, with LOD score > 4, and I find a few clusters of significant markers.
>
> Can I now run Interval Mapping in this situation? I do have a linkage map, which provides me with between-markers recombination frequencies.
>
> Any input would be greatly appreciated.
>
> Thanks!
> Dario

messages.author: a2e8310c8ee85c7c
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] interval mapping in an intercross
parts:
Hi Karl, 
Thank you for your reply. I did actually test whether the markers found were significant in 1,000,000 bootstrapped samples from the original population, where all the bootstrapped samples had median lifespan very close to that of the original population. This control-test allowed me to reduce the significant markers from 114 to 24. The current 24 significant markers are only significant among the long-lived individuals. 

I used this same analysis for another phenotype, i.e. color, and found 1 major QTL, which corresponds perfectly to the QTL found by R/qtl with IM. 

Would you have any suggestions on how to compute interval mapping by hand for my longevity trait? This would be greatly helpful. If you had time and prefer to talk to my over skype rather than by email I would greatly too, but if you cannot I perfectly understand that.  

Best regards, and thanks again for your reply. 

Dario

messages.author: 5523cb16ec47d553
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] interval mapping in an intercross
parts:
Hi Dario,

I believe your question fits closely with the work described in the paper Karl cited (Manichaikul A, Broman KW (2009) Binary trait mapping in experimental crosses with selective genotyping. Genetics182:863-874). In the paper, we present several approaches for the analysis of experimental crosses under selective genotyping, and also describe how to perform interval mapping in this case.  We implemented our methods in freely available code here:
http://people.virginia.edu/~am3xa/software.php

Please be in touch if you have any questions.
Ani

parts:
Dear Ani, 
I am running your rqtlMprob code and I keep on having this error :

#######################################################################################

# I first loaded G2_01_script.R

> library(qtl)
> library("qtlMprob", lib.loc="~/R/library/qtlMprob/")
> summary(g3.1_estrf0.1)
> g_cross<-g3.1_estrf0.1
> g_cross<-subset(g_cross, chr=1:20) # in this way I subset the whole cross object to 20 chromosomes
> summary(g_cross)
> g_cross$pheno$age <- ifelse(g_cross$pheno$days>=280,1,0)
> naff <- sum(g_cross$pheno$age==1, na.rm=T)
> nunaff <- sum(g_cross$pheno$age==0, na.rm=T)
> mymap <- pull.map(g_cross)

#generate data sets
> g_cross.aff <- subset(g_cross, ind=g_cross$pheno$age==1)
> both.index <- c(which(g_cross$pheno$age==1), which(g_cross$pheno$age==0)[sample(1:nunaff,naff)]) #ind for both
> g_cross.both <- subset(g_cross, ind=both.index)
> g_cross.both.missing <- g_cross
> for(chr in 1:20)  g_cross.both.missing$geno[[chr]]$data[-both.index,] <- NA

> g_cross <- calc.genoprob(g_cross, step=1)
> g_cross.aff <- calc.genoprob(g_cross.aff, step=1)
> g_cross.both <- calc.genoprob(g_cross.both, step=1)
> g_cross.both.missing <- calc.genoprob(g_cross.both.missing,step=1)

#genome scans
> g_cross.scan <- scanone(g_cross, pheno=3, chr=1:20, model="binary") #full genotypes
> maxlod.full <- max(g_cross.scan$lod)

> g_cross.aff.scan <- scanone.reverse(g_cross.aff, pheno.col=3, chr=1:20, phi.null="seg", step=1) #affected only
Error in if (count >= maxit | max(abs(phi.s1 - phi.s)) < tol) flag = 0 else count <- count +  : 
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
In addition: Warning message:
In scanone.reverse(g_cross.aff, pheno.col = 3, chr = 1:20, phi.null = "seg",  :
  First calculating genotype and marker probabilities.

#######################################################################################

Do you have any ideas about why this is happening?

I would greatly appreciate if you could help me figure out how to run your code. 

Thank you very much. 

Dario
